title: What's the 'were' in werewolf? | SPOOKY ETYMOLOGY

entries.note: A Scottish shortening of [[from:All Hallows' Eve]], the eve of [[see:All Saints' Day]], with roots in [[see:Samhain]] and Roman festivals like [[see:Feralia]].
A Christian festival on 1 November, created when [[see:Pope Gregory III]] expanded the earlier martyrs' day to celebrate all saints.
The pope who expanded the martyrs' day into [[see:All Saints' Day]].
Also called old year's night, the last night of the Celtic year, when the boundary between the living and the dead was thought to weaken.
Literally a bone fire; bonfires were lit during [[see:Samhain]] celebrations.
A Roman festival honouring the spirits of the dead, one of the Roman traditions that fed into [[see:Halloween]].
Roman goddess of fruit and trees who especially liked apples; her celebrations are said to be the source of [[see:bobbing for apples]].
Said to come from Roman celebrations honouring [[from?:Pomona]]; the hosts joke that it amounts to waterboarding yourself for an apple.
Rob first calls it a vegetable, then corrects himself: a gourd is a hard-shelled fruit.
Of Irish origin and older than America; Jack is a generic name, the 'o' could be various prepositions, and it once also meant [[see:will-o'-the-wisp]] or a lantern-carrier.
Britons just call a carved one a pumpkin, not a [[see:jack-o'-lantern]]; pumpkins are native to the Americas, so the first lanterns were [[see:turnip]]s.
A generic name for any man, like 'guy' today, and often a trickster figure in folk tales, such as [[see:Stingy Jack]].
A drunkard in a folk tale who twice traps Satan and ends up roaming the earth with a coal in a turnip; the tale postdates the name [[see:jack-o'-lantern]].
The first carved [[see:jack-o'-lantern]]s were turnips, like the one [[see:Stingy Jack]] put his coal in.
Will is a generic man's name and a wisp was a straw torch; it's a lurking light resembling a person with a lamp, also once called a [[see:jack-o'-lantern]].
A night of chaos on 30 October that caused a moral panic in 1950s–60s America; Britain's older version fell on 4 November, before [[see:Bonfire Night]].
The British night marking [[see:Guy Fawkes]]'s failed attempt to blow up the Houses of Parliament; the night before is a [[see:Mischief Night]].
Tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament, which is commemorated on [[see:Bonfire Night]]; the word [[gave:guy]] comes from him.
In every sense, including the effigy burned on bonfires, it comes from [[from:Guy Fawkes]]; the hosts plan to cover it in a future episode.
From Old English [[from:wicce]], feminine of [[from:wicca]]; originally not gendered, it became associated with women around the 1600s.
Once [[see:witch]] became associated with women, male witches were called he witches, which shows when the shift happened.
Like [[see:he witch]], a term for a male [[see:witch]] once the plain word came to imply a woman.
One of several Old English kinds of witch: someone who practises incantations or necromancy.
An Old English kind of witch who calls on phantoms and spirits.
An Old English kind of witch who works with drugs, potions, poisons and charms.
An adjective formed from the Old English word for a witch, which makes 'wicked witch' redundant; related to [[same-root:witch]].
The modern pagan belief system, named in the 20th century directly after the Old English word for a male [[same-root:witch]].
Not a male [[see:witch]] at first: from words for 'covenant' and 'lying', it meant an oathbreaker, then was applied to the devil.
Probably from the same Old English word as the second part of [[same-root?:warlock]]; compare Germanic forms like luga.
Someone using supernatural powers for good, rather than witchcraft, was simply called wise, reflecting a link between knowledge and magic.
Mock-Latin patter used by jugglers performing tricks; one 1694 claim derives it from [[from?:hoc est corpus meum]], another from [[from?:hax pax max Deus adimax]].
Real Latin from the Mass, which a 1694 writer said jugglers mocked to give [[gave?:hocus pocus]], taking a swipe at transubstantiation.
Another proposed source of [[see:hocus pocus]], which the hosts call gibberish.
Probably comes from [[from:hocus pocus]].
Jess notes that [[see:hoax]]es made it hard to work out where cocktail comes from.
A word that gets into a dictionary without ever existing, by mistake or deliberately to catch copiers; Rob recently made a video about them.
A fake word planted in the 2005 New Oxford American Dictionary, defined as wilful avoidance of one's official responsibilities.
A real word in the same dictionary, given as a contrast to the fake [[see:esquivalience]].
Another real entry in the dictionary that contained the fake [[see:esquivalience]].
An accidental ghost word for density, from a garbled 'D or d' slip by [[see:Austin M. Patterson]]; it stayed in print for years.
A deliberately planted fictitious entry, named after the fictional Virginia Mountweazel.
A fake dish in a US Army food survey that soldiers rated above lima beans and eggplant.
A made-up dish included in the same US Army survey as [[see:funistrada]] to test whether soldiers were paying attention.
A third made-up dish in the US Army survey, alongside [[see:funistrada]].
Merriam's chemistry editor, whose slip for 'D or d' (density) was lost, retyped and misread as [[see:dord]].
Discussed in an earlier episode, the source of collective nouns, including the misread [[see:business of ferrets]] that produced [[see:fesynes]].
A ghost word from a misreading, through bad handwriting, of 'business' in [[from:business of ferrets]].
A collective noun in the [[see:Book of St Albans]] whose garbled spelling produced [[gave:fesynes]].
The rarely used letter whose confusion with f produced [[gave:foup]].
A ghost word in [[see:Samuel Johnson]]'s dictionary, defined as to drive with sudden impetuosity; a [[see:long s]] misreading of [[from:soop]].
Put the ghost word [[see:foup]] in his dictionary, and later edited the first English text featuring [[see:vampire]].
The real word behind [[see:foup]], a dialect equivalent of [[equivalent:swoop]].
The standard equivalent of the dialect word [[equivalent:soop]].
A ghost word from [[see:The Monastery]], wildly glossed (from Latin 'to bite', 'to prime'), until the manuscript showed [[see:Walter Scott]] wrote [[see:nurse]].
Wrote 'nurse' in [[see:The Monastery]], which was misprinted as the ghost word [[see:morse]].
The [[see:Walter Scott]] novel whose line 'Dost thou so soon nurse thoughts of slaughter' was misprinted with [[see:morse]].
Source of the name Morse code, which came about 30 years after the ghost word [[unrelated:morse]].
The word Scott actually wrote, misread as the ghost word [[see:morse]].
A ghost word for an apparition, made by joining 'phantom nations' from [[see:Alexander Pope]]'s Homer translation into one word.
His Homer translation's 'all the phantom nations of the dead' was turned into [[gave:phantomnation]].
An old Germanic word that got its H from [[see:William Caxton]], copying Flemish; once meant breath or spirit, and only meant a dead person's apparition from the 14th century.
England's first printer, trained in Bruges, who added the Flemish H to [[see:ghost]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:ghost]] and also gained an H; from an Old English verb meaning to frighten, literally to gasp.
Like [[same-root:aghast]], shares a root with [[same-root:ghost]] and comes from an Old English verb meaning to frighten, with no original H.
Became prominent when [[see:Martin Luther]] listed poltergeists among Catholicism's corruptions for letting people contact the dead.
Father of Protestantism, whose list of Catholic evils made [[see:poltergeist]] prominent.
Keeps the old breath or spirit sense of [[see:ghost]]; Old English used a phrase with gast for God.
Named with the [[see:Holy Ghost]] as keeping the old breath or spirit sense.
From Latin [[from:spiritus]], breath of a god, once translated as [[see:ghost]]; both later came to mean a see-through apparition.
From an Arabic word for a body-snatching, flesh-eating spirit, from a verb meaning to seize; it entered English through [[see:Vathek]].
The Arabic word for a female [[see:ghoul]].
Simply the Dutch word; modern Dutch uses it for [[see:ghost]].
William Beckford's orientalist novel, first written in French, whose translation brought [[see:ghoul]] into English.
British slang for testicles, from a Hindi word for bullet; unrelated to [[unrelated:ghoul]].
Nothing to do with horses: from Old English [[from:mare]], a goblin that sat on sleepers, probably reflecting night terrors or sleep paralysis.
Old English for a goblin or [[see:incubus]], probably from a root meaning to harm; replaced in the 1600s, surviving only in [[gave:nightmare]].
The male counterpart of a [[see:succubus]], a demon that visits sleepers to seduce them; it replaced [[see:mare]] in the 1600s.
The female counterpart of an [[see:incubus]], a night-visiting seducer that helped replace [[see:mare]].
The French [[equivalent:nightmare]]: the first part means to press, describing the oppressive feeling of something sitting on you, and the second matches [[same-root:mare]].
The German [[equivalent:nightmare]], literally elf dream.
Originally meant to frequent, as in Middle English 'haunt school', a sense surviving in 'your usual haunt'.
A Slavonic word, perhaps Russian, that came to English through French and German writing after a 1720s Serbian vampire craze; first seen in a manuscript [[see:Samuel Johnson]] edited.
Romanian for son of [[from:Vlad Dracul]] or of the dragon; [[see:Bram Stoker]] named his vampire after [[see:Vlad the Impaler]]. Jess calls the novel full of plot holes.
Author who popularised [[see:Dracula]] as a vampire name, taking it from [[see:Vlad the Impaler]].
The real Wallachian prince, called Vlad Dracula, who impaled victims and supposedly dipped bread in their blood; [[see:Dracula]] was named after him.
Father of [[see:Vlad the Impaler]], possibly called 'dragon' after joining the [[see:Order of the Dragon]].
A group of Christian knights that [[see:Vlad Dracul]] joined, one theory for the dragon link in [[see:Dracula]].
Means beyond the forest; its 'sylvania' matches [[same-root:Pennsylvania]], and 'trans' works as in [[see:transatlantic]].
Contains the same forest element as [[same-root:Transylvania]].
Forest elves, sharing the forest element of [[same-root:Transylvania]].
Means families of the forest, using the same element as [[same-root:Transylvania]].
Compared with [[see:Transylvania]]: 'trans' means across or on the other side.
The Texan in [[see:Dracula]] whom Jess calls a ninja cowboy, because he speaks in scenes without ever being introduced.
A [[see:Dracula]] character whose English swings between fluent and awkward as the plot needs, one of the novel's inconsistencies.
The film adaptation of [[see:Dracula]]; possibly from Romanian [[from?:nesuferitul]], insufferable one, or Greek [[from?:nosophoros]], disease carrier.
A very old word, most likely man-wolf from Old English [[from:wer]], man; a 1425 text implies a fanciful 'beware' explanation that the hosts reject.
A female [[see:werewolf]] would be a 'wif wolf', from Old English wif, woman, the source of wife; wer and wif appear paired in manuscripts.
A very old word, from when wolves troubled the Anglo-Saxons; its plural keeps the Old English f-to-v shift between vowels, as in [[see:knife]].
Its plural knives shows the same Old English f-to-v change as [[see:wolf]].
Another plural showing the f-to-v change seen in [[see:wolf]].
Another plural showing the f-to-v change seen in [[see:wolf]].
Literally bee wolf, a kenning for a bear: a big fluffy [[see:wolf]] that likes honey.
First meant a divine omen or sign, from Latin roots meaning to warn and to show, like [[same-root:demonstrate]]; by English it meant a disfigured person.
Shares the Latin 'show' verb with [[same-root:monster]]; Jess says it contains no demon but does contain a monster.
The French verb 'to show', linked to [[same-root:monster]].
